data.title: Autistic-like behaviour and cerebellar dysfunction in Purkinje cell Tsc1 mutant mice
data.authors: Tsai PT; Hull C; Chu Y; Greene-Colozzi E; Sadowski AR; Leech JM; Steinberg J; Crawley JN; Regehr WG; Sahin M

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: L7Cre;Tsc1 flox mice (Purkinje-cell-specific heterozygous and homozygous Tsc1 deletion); cerebellar slice electrophysiology; behaviour; rapamycin from P7
data.finding: Deleting one or both copies of Tsc1 only in cerebellar Purkinje cells raised phospho-S6 (a readout of mTORC1) in those cells. Both heterozygous and homozygous mutants showed autism-like behaviour: no preference for a mouse over an object or for a new mouse, more self-grooming, more pup ultrasonic calls and poorer reversal learning in a water T-maze. Purkinje cells fired fewer action potentials, both spontaneously and when driven, in a gene-dose-dependent way, while their synaptic inputs looked largely normal; homozygous mutants also lost Purkinje cells from about 2 months of age and became ataxic. Rapamycin (6 mg/kg intraperitoneally, three times a week from postnatal day 7) prevented the Purkinje cell loss and enlargement and the social, learning and motor deficits. Boundary: mouse, cell-type-specific genetic deletion; rapamycin given from early postnatal life, so this is prevention, not reversal; relevance to human autism is by analogy with TSC patients.
data.abstract_excerpt: Autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are highly prevalent neurodevelopmental disorders, but the underlying pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Recent studies have implicated the cerebellum in these disorders, with post-mortem studies in ASD patients showing cerebellar Purkinje cell (PC) loss, and isolated cerebellar injury has been associated with a higher incidence of ASDs. However, the extent of cerebellar contribution to the pathogenesis of ASDs remains unclear.

extracted_findings.effect: Tsc1 loss in Purkinje cells caused autism-like behaviour and reduced PC excitability; rapamycin prevented the deficits
